senses.definition: One who, or that which, hooks.
(rugby) A player who hooks the ball out of the scrum with his foot.

quotes.text: Hooker Dylan Hartley was sent to the sin-bin after yet another infringement at the breakdown and, on the stroke of half-time, Georgia's territorial advantage finally told when number eight Basilaia surged over from the base of the scrum for a try next to the posts.
quotes.reference: 2011 September 18, Ben Dirs, “Rugby World Cup 2011: England 41-10 Georgia”, in BBC Sport:

senses.definition: (cricket) A batsman or batswoman adept at or fond of playing hook shots.

quotes.text: I once saw Hassett drop England opening batsman and compulsive hooker, Cyril Washbrook, twice in succession at deep fine leg.
quotes.reference: 1990, Ashes: Battles and Bellylaughs, Byron Bay: Swan Publishing, page 32:

senses.definition: (informal, dated) Synonym of hook (“attention-grabbing element of a creative work”).

quotes.text: We regard the first seven seconds of a television commercial as the most critical or crucial in the whole unit — the "Do or Die Seven" — the "moment of decision" or the "hooker", if you will, when we must capture the attention of the viewer, get him involved in the action, […]
quotes.reference: 1966, Charles Anthony Wainwright, The Television Copywriter, page 39:

senses.definition: (archaic, thieves' cant) A thief who uses a pole with a hook on the end to steal goods.

quotes.text: They are sure to be clyd in the night by the angler, or hooker, or such like pilferers that liue upon the spoyle of other poore people.
quotes.reference: c. 1608–1610, Samuel Rid, Martin Mark-all, Beadle of Bridewell:

quotes.text: Suffer none, from far or near, / With their rights to interfere; / No strange Abram, Ruffler crack— / Hooker of another pack—
quotes.reference: 1834, William Harrison Ainsworth, Rookwood, volume 2, Oath of the Canting Crew, page 339:

quotes.text: All my life, been hustling / And tonight is my appraisal / 'Cause I'm a hooker selling songs / And my pimp's a record label

senses.definition: (slang, dated, 1920s to 1940s) An imprecise measure of alcoholic drink; a "slug" (of gin), or an overlarge gulp.

quotes.text: Emily had cut short these 3 A.M. glooms with a hooker of bourbon.

quotes.text: [T]he poor Flash is gone, and there is an end of it. Poor old hooker. Hey, Almayer? You made a voyage or two with me. Wasn’t she a sweet craft?
